narrative:
The model determined that you have an 83.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students, signaled that you would likely struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your family income bracket was the third most important factor and worked mildly in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not nearly large enough to offset the impact of your low class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 30 and undergraduate GPA of 2.60, both well below the averages of accepted students, further reinforced the model’s concern, though they were not the dominant drivers.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving these areas will be the most direct way to increase your chances of passing the bar and gaining admission in a future application cycle. (218 words)
